changelog: Replace E1 with measured example ja_jp_968 to teach the model that cuts isolating the sentence-final predicate/auxiliary are very bad (addresses the primary finding).
Replace E2 with measured example ja_jp_563 to show a short-latency case where trailing auxiliaries/negation flip meaning and should be ranked low.
Replace E3 with measured example ja_jp_1584 to provide a mid-latency instance demonstrating predicate continuation risks when cutting before clause-final material.
Replace E4 with measured example ja_jp_919 to provide a long-latency example where separating final predicate/punctuation harms cohesion and should be penalized.
findings: The scorer routinely allows cuts that isolate sentence-final predicates/auxiliaries, negation, or closing punctuation as their own right-hand fragment — these positions nearly always flip or void the left fragment and should be treated as very bad cuts.

The instruction to 'spread distinct integers across the full 0–100 range' pushes scorers to exaggerate separations and prevents clustering of many equally poor (or equally good) positions; this interacts badly with short‑latency bins and thins needed dense cuts.

diagnosis.why: Replacing the four examples with measured Japanese cases that penalize isolating sentence-final predicates/auxiliaries moved the model away from placing cuts immediately before clause-final material, yielding most of the measured gain in the mid-to-long latency bins (≤7–≤10). However the model overcorrected in many instances by shifting cuts into internal morpheme/character boundaries (fragmenting words and particles), producing the large negative tail moves despite the net positive bin-level effect.
diagnosis.lesson: Keep the emphasis that cutting off clause‑final predicates/auxiliaries is harmful, but avoid example edits that encourage overcorrection into internal-word/particle fragmentation.
